content: The text provided is a long list of references and excluded studies related to the prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV, focusing on antiretroviral therapy (ART) and infant feeding practices. 1. A controlled trial published in The Lancet in 2012 (Volume 379, Issue 9812, Pages 221-228) investigated the outcomes of antiretroviral therapy in preventing mother-to-child transmission of HIV. 2. Thakwalakwa et al. conducted a randomized trial in Malawi to assess the growth and HIV-free survival of HIV-exposed infants. The study compared two complementary feeding interventions in the context of maternal antiretroviral therapy, as published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2014 (Volume 66, Issue 2, Pages 181-187). 3. Jamieson et al. evaluated maternal and infant antiretroviral regimens to prevent postnatal HIV-1 transmission. The study followed participants for 48 weeks as part of the BAN randomized controlled trial, with findings published in The Lancet in 2012 (Volume 379, Issue 9835, Pages 2449-2458). 4. Thomas et al. examined the efficacy of triple-antiretroviral prophylaxis in preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission through breastfeeding. This clinical trial, known as the Kisumu Breastfeeding Study, was conducted in Kenya and published in PLOS Medicine in 2011 (Volume 8, Issue 3, Article e1001015). 5. Alvarez-Uria et al. analyzed the effects of formula feeding and breastfeeding on child growth, infant mortality, and HIV transmission among children born to HIV-infected mothers receiving triple antiretroviral therapy in resource-limited settings. The study, conducted in India, was published in ISRN Pediatrics in 2012 (Article ID 763591). 6. Marazzi et al. reported increased HIV-free survival rates at one year of age among infants in sub-Saharan Africa whose mothers used highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) during breastfeeding. The findings were published in the Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal in 2009 (Volume 28, Issue 6, Pages 483-487). 7. Kilewo et al. investigated the prevention of mother-to-child HIV-1 transmission through breastfeeding by treating mothers with triple antiretroviral therapy in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. The Mitra Plus study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2009 (Volume 52, Issue 3, Pages 406-416). 8. Peltier et al. compared breastfeeding with maternal antiretroviral therapy versus formula feeding to prevent postnatal HIV transmission in Rwanda. The study was published in AIDS in 2009 (Volume 23, Issue 18, Pages 2415-2423). 9. Ngoma et al. evaluated the efficacy of the WHO recommendation for continued breastfeeding and maternal combination antiretroviral therapy (cART) in preventing perinatal and postnatal HIV transmission in Zambia. The findings were published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society in 2015 (Volume 18, Article 19352). 10. Sagay et al. assessed mother-to-child transmission outcomes among HIV-exposed infants followed in Jos, North-Central Nigeria. The study was published in Current HIV Research in 2015 (Volume 13, Issue 3, Pages 193-200). 11. Giuliano et al. examined maternal antiretroviral therapy for preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission in Malawi, focusing on maternal and infant outcomes two years after delivery. The study was published in PLOS One in 2013 (Volume 8, Issue 7, Article e68950). 12. A comprehensive search strategy was employed in PubMed to identify relevant studies on maternal antiretroviral therapy, HIV transmission, and infant feeding practices. The search included terms such as maternal, antiretroviral therapy, HIV, transmission, breastfeeding, and postnatal, with a publication date range from 2005 to 2015. 13. Several studies were excluded from the analysis due to insufficient data on HIV transmission rates at six months, lack of adherence to feeding and ART protocols, or focus on unrelated outcomes such as mortality or cost-effectiveness. 14. For example, studies like the Kesho-Bora trial and others in Burkina Faso, Kenya, and South Africa did not provide transmission rates at six months or detailed data on ART and breastfeeding practices. 15. Other excluded studies, such as those by Cohan et al. and Lawani et al., focused on adherence challenges or compared ART regimens without providing transmission rates specific to breastfeeding mothers. 16. Studies like those by Shapiro et al. and Homsy et al. were excluded because they did not provide data on HIV transmission rates at six months or combined ART and breastfeeding outcomes. 17. Additional studies, such as those by Tonwe-Gold et al. and Seth et al., were excluded due to small sample sizes, lack of detailed ART regimens, or insufficient data on breastfeeding practices. 18. The excluded studies highlight the challenges in obtaining comprehensive data on the combined effects of ART and breastfeeding in preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission, particularly in resource-limited settings. 19. The findings underscore the importance of robust study designs and standardized reporting to evaluate the efficacy of PMTCT interventions effectively.
